subject: Critical Thinking
title: Strong vs. Weak Induction
description: A short lesson to help you apply Strong vs. Weak Induction.

hook.text: 'I met two rude New Yorkers, so all New Yorkers are rude.' That's induction — very, very bad induction.

buildup.text: Strong induction: large, representative sample + conclusion that doesn't overreach the evidence.

discovery.text: Weak induction: small sample, biased sample, or conclusion that leaps far beyond what the data supports.

twist.text: Sample size matters, but representativeness matters more. A million biased data points are still biased.

climax.text: The strength of induction is a spectrum. Learning to judge where you are on it is a superpower.

punchline.text: Not all generalizations are equal. Some are earned.

quiz.question: What makes inductive reasoning 'strong'?
options: Large representative sample with proportionate conclusions

details.summary: Inductive arguments range from strong to weak depending on how well the evidence supports the conclusion. A strong inductive argument makes its conclusion very probable; a weak one leaves significant room for doubt.
details.whyItMatters: Evaluating inductive strength is essential for assessing scientific studies, statistical claims, and everyday generalizations.
takeaways: Inductive strength is a spectrum, not a binary
Sample size, diversity, and relevance determine strength
Even strong induction does not provide certainty

faq.question: What makes an inductive argument strong versus weak?
faq.answer: Strong induction has large, representative samples and relevant evidence that makes the conclusion highly probable. Weak induction relies on small, biased, or irrelevant samples.

faq.question: Can a strong inductive argument have a false conclusion?
faq.answer: Yes. Strength means the conclusion is very likely given the premises, but induction never reaches certainty. New evidence can always overturn even the strongest inductive conclusion.
